title: Dimon Says JPMorgan Is 'All-In' on Growth in China
description: Mar.14 -- Jamie Dimon, chief executive officer at JPMorgan, discusses the "tough road" ahead for China and his firm's approach to growing its business in the nation. He speaks with Bloomberg's Francine Lacqua at the JPMorgan 2019 Global Markets Conference on "Bloomberg Daybreak: Americas."

asr.full_text: How worried are you on China? How should we look at China? And what kind of business do you want to do in China? So China, first of all, the trade issues are real. They need to be resolved. They need to be resolved across all these issues. I think the administration is doing the right— Will they be resolved? We expect so. We think both parties want it, but they're complex. They're talking about having hundreds of pages of memorandums and understandings so far. If it doesn't get resolved, I there is a reason to be worried about China will be a fully developed nation in 30 years and it's economy is going to be as big as the United States but it still has a tough road. They're very smart but they don't have enough food war and energy, they have huge corruption,and the market you have here in terms of research and capability knowledge and rule of law doesn't have all of that there yet. It's not a criticism're going to have a way to go. So they'll grow now, but there'll be times in the future, five years out, where there'll be real bumps in the road in China. Okay, so what does that mean, that as an investor in China, you kind of slow down for four or five years until you see the lay of the land, or do you just go all in to get market share? We're all in, and so we're not slowing down. People are slowing down because of trade, not because of what I just said. But my point is that when they do have problems, you know, they might be building up huge imbalances in the financial system. That will come home to roost one day. Right now they can handle it. China's not like the rest of our countries. They can macro manage. They can simply tell the fiscal people, tell the monetary people, tell the companies what they need to do, who they need to hire, but that won't always be true. And so one day, these imbalances may cause a disruption. Call it a recession. But a financial crisis kind of disruption? It could be. We had a financial crisis, you know, and markets panic. They can handle that today, but I'm saying in five or seven years, they have to be careful building up imbalances. Because the bigger the markets get, the less they can control all the things that they would want to control to stop that from happening. So I'm not going to say it's going to happen, but we're so used to China going at 6%, 7%, that the second they don't, I think the world will react probably more scared than they should be.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it presents a Bloomberg interview about China's economic conditions, trade issues, JPMorgan's business growth, and related market risks. The discussion of being "all in" on growth in China describes corporate strategy and economic outlook rather than soliciting money, credentials, or participation from viewers. The speaker also qualifies potential outcomes by saying he is not certain a disruption will occur, supporting a market-commentary context rather than a guaranteed financial claim.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The primary content is financial news and market analysis: the interview covers China's trade issues, economic imbalances, JPMorgan's business strategy and possible future disruption, while the speaker qualifies the forecast rather than presenting a guaranteed outcome.
